title: Object Storage Service
prompt: Design an object store like S3: users create buckets and put, get, list and delete files of any size, from a few bytes to terabytes. Data must essentially never be lost.

clarify.q: What durability target, and what failures must we survive: disks, racks, a whole datacenter?
clarify.why: Surviving a full zone loss means spreading every object across zones. That decides the erasure-code layout and cross-zone bandwidth costs.

clarify.q: What is the object size distribution?
clarify.why: Billions of 4 KB objects stress metadata and per-object overhead. Terabyte objects need multipart upload. Most real systems have both, and they need different handling.

clarify.q: Read-after-write consistency for new objects, overwrites and listings?
clarify.why: Strong consistency needs a single authoritative metadata commit per key. Eventual consistency is cheaper but confuses clients that write then list.

clarify.q: Do we need versioning and object lifecycle rules?
clarify.why: Versioning turns overwrites into appends of new versions, which changes the metadata key and garbage collection.

clarify.q: How much data and how many requests at peak?
clarify.why: Petabytes decide the replication versus erasure coding cost. Request rates size the metadata tier, which is usually the real bottleneck.

clarify.q: Single region, or replicated across regions?
clarify.why: Cross-region replication is asynchronous in practice. Saying so keeps the core design to one region with several zones.

functional: Create and delete buckets. Put, get (including byte ranges), head and delete objects by key.
List objects in a bucket by prefix, with a delimiter to browse like folders, paginated.
Upload large objects in parts, in parallel, with resume.
Access control per bucket and object (owner, policies, signed URLs).
nonFunctional: Durability: annual chance of losing a given object below 10^-11 under independent disk failures, and survive the loss of one zone.
Availability 99.99% for reads and writes in a region.
Strong read-after-write: after a successful PUT, every GET and LIST sees the new object.
First-byte latency p99 under 100 ms for small objects; throughput scales with parallel range reads.
Storage overhead at most 1.5× raw bytes per logical byte for large objects.
outOfScope: CDN in front of the store.

assumptions: 100 B objects, average size 1 MB (heavily skewed: most objects small, most bytes in big ones)
Peak 300 k GET/s and 30 k PUT/s; average GET returns 256 KB
Disks are 20 TB; servers hold 24 disks; annual disk failure rate (AFR) 2%
Erasure code 8+4: 8 data fragments, 4 parity, any 8 of 12 rebuild the object
Repair window (time to rebuild a lost fragment) 24 hours, simple independent-failure model

steps.label: Disks and servers (before free-space headroom)
steps.math: 150 PB / 20 TB = 7 500 disks / 24 ≈ 313 servers. Replication: 15 000 disks, 625 servers

steps.label: Metadata size
steps.result: 50 TB, 150 TB with 3 replicas. Needs a sharded metadata tier.

steps.label: Read bandwidth
steps.result: ≈ 614 Gbps out, ≈ 2 Gbps per storage server

steps.label: Chance a disk fails during one repair window
Annual loss probability per object
steps.result: Erasure 8+4 is about 28× more durable at half the raw storage

estimates.takeaway: Storage cost points to erasure coding: half the disks of triple replication and still more durable. The durability math also shows the strongest lever is the repair window: loss with 8+4 scales with p³, so repairing in 1 hour instead of 24 makes loss 24³ ≈ 14 000 times less likely. Metadata is 50 TB and takes every request, so it gets its own sharded, strongly consistent tier. Real failures are correlated (racks, power, bad batches of disks), so fragment placement across racks and zones matters as much as the formula.

api.note: Returns only after data fragments are durable and metadata is committed. Checksum verified end to end.
Ranges let clients read big objects in parallel.
Lexicographic order. nextToken encodes the last key returned.
Parts upload in parallel and can be retried independently.
Complete: atomically makes the object visible. A separate DELETE aborts and frees parts.

entities.name: ObjectMeta
entities.store: Range-partitioned replicated KV (Raft groups), key = bucket + key + version
entities.why: Sorted keys make prefix LIST a range scan. Raft gives a single strongly consistent commit point per key.

entities.name: Extent
fields: append-only until sealed at about 1 GB
entities.why: Big append-only containers. Small objects are packed into them, so the placement map tracks millions of extents instead of billions of objects.

entities.name: Fragment
entities.store: Local disk on a data node
fields: detect bit rot on read and scrub
entities.why: The data node knows nothing about buckets or keys, only fragments.

entities.name: MultipartUpload
entities.store: Same metadata KV, separate key space
entities.why: Parts stay invisible until complete, then their chunk lists become one object's chunk list.

data.note: Three layers of mapping: key → chunks (metadata, 50 TB, sharded), extent → fragment locations (placement, small), and fragment → bytes (data nodes). The metadata store is partitioned by key range, not hash, because LIST by prefix must scan keys in order; ranges split automatically when they get large or hot. Each range is a Raft group of 3 replicas in 3 zones, so a metadata write commits once a majority (2 of 3) has it.

hld.summary:
Clients talk to stateless front-end servers that authenticate, authorize, and orchestrate. For a PUT, the front end streams the bytes into an open extent: it splits each stripe into 8 data fragments, computes 4 parity fragments, and writes all 12 to data nodes chosen by the placement service across racks and zones. Once at least the required fragments are durable, it commits a metadata record in the metadata service; that commit is the moment the object exists. For a GET, the front end reads metadata, then reads any 8 fragments in parallel and decodes, or reads only the data fragments when all are healthy.

Background services keep it healthy: a repair service rebuilds fragments after disk failures, a scrubber reads every fragment periodically to catch silent corruption, and a garbage collector compacts extents whose objects were deleted. Metadata and data scale independently, which is the core of the design.

diagram.title: Object store components
diagram.src:
flowchart LR
  C[Client] --> LB[Load balancer]
  LB --> FE[Front-end servers]
  FE --> MD[(Metadata service, range shards)]
  FE --> PL[Placement service]
  FE --> DN1[Data nodes zone A]
  FE --> DN2[Data nodes zone B]
  FE --> DN3[Data nodes zone C]
  RP[Repair and scrub] --> PL
  RP --> DN1
  GC[Garbage collector] --> MD
  GC --> PL

flows.title: PUT a 4 MB object
steps: Front end authenticates the signed request and checks the bucket policy.
Placement gives an open extent with 12 fragment locations: 4 per zone, each on a different rack.
Front end encodes the bytes into 8 data + 4 parity fragments and writes all 12 in parallel. It waits for all 12, or for 11 and lets repair fill the last one.
Front end commits ObjectMeta (bucket, key, version, chunks, etag) to the metadata Raft group. Only now is the object visible.
Returns 200 with the etag. A crash before the commit leaves orphan bytes that GC later reclaims; the object was never visible.

flows.title: GET with a dead disk
steps: Front end reads ObjectMeta and the extent's fragment map.
It requests the 8 data fragments; one disk is dead, so it also requests a parity fragment.
With any 8 fragments it decodes the stripe, verifies the checksum, and streams bytes to the client.
It reports the dead fragment to repair, which rebuilds it elsewhere.

flows.title: Disk failure and repair
steps: Data node heartbeat shows a dead disk holding about 20 TB of fragments.
Repair lists affected extents and rebuilds each missing fragment by reading 8 others and decoding.
Work is spread across hundreds of nodes, so a 20 TB disk is rebuilt in about an hour instead of the 28 hours a single replacement disk would need (20 TB at 200 MB/s = 100 000 s).
Extents with more missing fragments are repaired first.

deepDives.title: Separating the metadata service from data nodes
deepDives.problem: Metadata and data have opposite shapes. Metadata is small (500 bytes per object), random access, needs strong consistency and sorted listing. Data is huge, sequential, write-once. Putting both in one system either wastes fast storage on bytes or puts slow disks on every lookup.

options.name: Separate tiers: sorted replicated KV for metadata, simple fragment stores for data
options.how: Metadata in a range-sharded, Raft-replicated KV on SSD. Data nodes only store fragments by id on HDDs.
pros: Each tier scales and fails independently
Data nodes are dumb and cheap
Metadata commit gives one clear moment of consistency
cons: Two systems to run
Every request does a metadata lookup first, so the metadata tier must be very fast

options.name: Hash the key straight to data nodes, metadata stored with the data
options.how: Consistent hashing on bucket+key picks nodes; each node stores bytes and metadata.
pros: No separate metadata lookup
Simple to start
cons: LIST by prefix must ask every node
Changing the ring moves bytes, not just pointers
Strong consistency per key needs quorum logic on data nodes

deepDives.choice: Separate tiers. 300 k metadata reads/s across thousands of range shards is routine for SSD-backed KV; one shard at 5 k reads/s means about 60 hot shards' worth of load, spread over many more. The metadata write is the commit point, which gives strong read-after-write: if the commit succeeded, any later GET or LIST reads it from the Raft leader. CAP-wise the metadata tier is CP: if a range loses its majority, writes to that key range fail rather than diverge. I'd move to hashing only for a pure key-value blob store with no listing requirement.

deepDives.title: Erasure coding vs replication, with the durability math
deepDives.problem: At 100 PB, the redundancy scheme decides whether we buy 300 PB or 150 PB of disks. It also decides how much data is lost when disks fail together, and how expensive repair is.

options.name: 3× replication
options.how: Store three full copies on three racks or zones.
pros: Reads from any one copy; repair copies one replica
Low latency and CPU for small objects
cons: 3× storage
Annual loss per object ≈ 1.8 × 10^-10 in our model; tolerates only 2 failures

options.name: Erasure coding 8+4
options.how: Split into 8 data fragments, add 4 parity; any 8 of 12 recover the data. Place 4 per zone so a full zone loss leaves exactly 8.
pros: 1.5× storage
Tolerates any 4 failures; loss ≈ 6.5 × 10^-12 per object-year in our model
cons: Repair reads 8 fragments to rebuild 1 (8× repair traffic)
Degraded reads need decoding
After a zone loss there is no remaining margin until repair

options.name: Wider codes, for example 12+4 or 17+3
pros: Lower overhead (1.33× or less)
cons: More nodes touched per read and repair
Fewer failures tolerated relative to width

deepDives.choice: Erasure coding 8+4 for large data, replication for small and hot data. Math: with AFR 2% and a 24 h repair window, p = 0.02 × 24 / 8 760 ≈ 5.5 × 10^-5. Replication loses an object if, after one copy fails, the other two also fail inside the window: about 3 × 0.02 × p² ≈ 1.8 × 10^-10 per year. 8+4 needs 3 more of the other 11 to fail: 12 × 0.02 × 165 × p³ ≈ 6.5 × 10^-12. Across 10^11 objects that is about 0.65 versus 18 expected losses a year under independence, so we also cut the repair window: declustered repair across hundreds of nodes brings it near 1 hour, making 8+4 loss about 14 000 times smaller. Small objects (under 1 MB) are first written 3× replicated for low latency and packed into erasure-coded extents later. If storage were cheap and latency critical, I'd keep more data replicated.

deepDives.title: Multipart upload
deepDives.problem: A single PUT of a 200 GB file over one connection takes hours, cannot be parallelized, and must restart from zero on any network blip. We also must not show a half-uploaded object.

options.name: Multipart: independent parts, atomic complete
options.how: Initiate returns uploadId. Client uploads parts (5 MB to 5 GB) in parallel; each is stored as normal erasure-coded data and gets an etag. Complete sends the ordered list of part numbers and etags; metadata writes one ObjectMeta whose chunk list is the parts' chunks concatenated.
pros: Parallel throughput, retry one part not the whole file
No copying at complete: only metadata changes
Object appears atomically
cons: Orphaned parts from abandoned uploads cost storage until cleaned
Object etag is not a plain checksum of the whole file

options.name: Resumable single stream with offsets
options.how: Client streams and can resume from the last acknowledged offset.
pros: Simple client
cons: No parallelism; one slow path limits the whole upload
Server must track partial state per stream

deepDives.choice: Multipart. A 200 GB file in 100 MB parts is 2 000 parts; at 16 parallel uploads of 50 MB/s each, it takes about 200 GB / 800 MB/s = 250 s instead of over an hour on one stream. Complete is a single metadata transaction, so it is atomic and fast whatever the size. A lifecycle rule aborts uploads idle for 7 days and GC frees their parts. If clients were mostly small mobile uploads, I'd keep single PUT as the default and suggest multipart above about 100 MB.

diagram.title: Multipart upload sequence
diagram.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client
  participant F as Front end
  participant M as Metadata
  participant D as Data nodes
  C->>F: initiate upload
  F->>M: create upload record
  F-->>C: uploadId
  par part 1
    C->>F: part 1 bytes
    F->>D: encode and write fragments
    F->>M: record part 1 chunks and etag
    F-->>C: etag 1
  and part 2
    C->>F: part 2 bytes
    F->>D: encode and write fragments
    F->>M: record part 2 chunks and etag
    F-->>C: etag 2
  end
  C->>F: complete with parts 1 and 2 and etags
  F->>M: one txn, build object from part chunks
  F-->>C: 200 final etag

deepDives.title: Listing at scale
deepDives.problem: A bucket can hold billions of keys. Users list 'folders' with a prefix and delimiter, paginated, in sorted order. A bucket whose keys start with a timestamp sends every new write to the same end of the key space.

options.name: Range-partitioned sorted metadata
options.how: Keys sorted by bucket + key. LIST is a range scan from prefix, returning up to 1 000 keys. With a delimiter, the scan skips ahead past each common prefix (for example jump from photos/2025/ to the first key after photos/2025/\xff).
pros: Listing cost proportional to the page size, not bucket size
Natural pagination token: the last key returned
cons: Sequential keys create a hot range at the tail
Range splits and moves need careful leader handoff

options.name: Hash-partitioned metadata with scatter-gather list
options.how: Hash bucket+key to shards; LIST asks every shard and merges sorted results.
pros: Writes spread perfectly, no hot ranges
cons: Every LIST touches every shard of the bucket
Pagination needs a cursor per shard

options.name: Separate listing index updated asynchronously
options.how: Point reads use hash-partitioned metadata; a sorted index is built from a change stream.
pros: Fast point lookups and cheap writes
cons: LIST lags behind PUT, breaking strong list-after-write

deepDives.choice: Range-partitioned metadata, because strong list-after-write and ordered pagination are requirements. Hot tails are handled by automatic split on load: when a range's write rate passes a threshold, split at the median key and move the new range's leader to a different host. For a pathological pattern (one bucket writing 50 k sequential keys/s) we also document that adding a short random prefix spreads load. If listing could be eventually consistent, I'd use the async index and hash-partitioned point lookups for higher write throughput.

deepDives.title: Small objects, deletes and garbage collection
deepDives.problem: A 4 KB object erasure-coded on its own would become 12 fragments of about 512 bytes, each a separate disk write and file. Billions of them would overwhelm data node file systems. Deletes are also tricky: bytes live inside shared extents and cannot just be removed.

options.name: Pack objects into append-only extents, compact later
options.how: Objects are appended to an open extent (about 1 GB); when full it is sealed and erasure-coded. Delete only removes metadata. GC tracks live bytes per extent and rewrites extents below, say, 60% live.
pros: Few large files on disk, sequential writes
Delete is a cheap metadata op
cons: Space is reclaimed late
Compaction costs read and write bandwidth

options.name: One file per object on data nodes
options.how: Store each object or fragment as its own file.
pros: Delete frees space immediately
cons: Billions of small files exhaust inodes and make scrubbing slow
Per-object erasure coding is wasteful for tiny objects

deepDives.choice: Pack and compact. Writes are fast appends; delete is a metadata change (and a delete marker when versioning is on). GC compares extent live bytes with metadata and compacts the worst extents first, rate-limited so it never steals more than about 10% of node bandwidth. A safety rule: never reclaim bytes until a full metadata scan confirms no object version still references them, since a GC bug is the easiest way to lose data in this design. If the workload were almost all large objects, I'd skip packing and erasure-code each object directly.

failures: Fragments rebuilt from 8 others across many nodes, highest-risk extents first. Reads keep working via degraded decode meanwhile.
Each extent still has 8 of 12 fragments; reads decode. Metadata Raft groups keep a 2-of-3 majority. Writes go to the two healthy zones with a temporary 2-zone placement, rebalanced later.
Silent bit rot on a disk
Per-block checksums verified on every read and by a scrubber that reads all data every few weeks. Corrupt fragments are rebuilt like lost ones.
Front end crashes after writing fragments but before metadata commit
The object never became visible; client retries. GC finds unreferenced bytes in extents and reclaims them.
Raft elects a new leader in seconds; requests to that range retry. No acknowledged write is lost because it was on a majority.
A bad firmware batch makes many disks of one model fail together
Mix disk models and batches across each extent's placement; alert on per-model failure rate spikes; widen repair priority.
scale: 10× data (1 EB): add storage servers; placement prefers new nodes until balanced. Repair bandwidth grows with failures, so reserve network for it.
10× requests: metadata ranges split further; add a read cache for hot ObjectMeta (with invalidation on commit) and for hot small objects.
Cold data: move rarely read extents to wider codes (like 16+4) on denser disks; reads are slower but storage overhead drops to 1.25×.
Multi-region: async replication of committed objects by a change stream; each region is still strongly consistent locally.

followups.q: How do you give strong consistency on overwrite of the same key?
answer: Each PUT writes new fragments to new locations, then commits metadata.
The metadata commit for the key is linearizable through its Raft group, so the last commit wins and all readers see it.
Old version's bytes stay until GC, so in-flight readers of the old version still finish.

followups.q: How would you serve a very hot object (a viral image)?
answer: Cache it in front-end memory or a cache tier with its etag as part of the key.
Replicate hot small objects to more nodes temporarily.
Point customers at a CDN; the store sets cache headers.
Server signs method, bucket, key and expiry with the user's secret using an HMAC.
Front end recomputes the signature and checks expiry before serving.
No session needed; anyone with the URL can do that one action until it expires.

followups.q: How do you know the durability target is actually met?
answer: Track real disk failure rates, repair times, and how many extents sat with 1, 2 or 3 missing fragments.
Feed those into the same formula and into simulation with correlated failures.
Scrub results show silent corruption rates; alert when any extent drops to its last spare fragment.

followups.q: Where does CAP show up here?
answer: Metadata is CP: a range without a majority rejects writes rather than diverge.
Data fragments tolerate failures by redundancy, not by relaxing consistency.
Cross-region replication is AP: each region stays available and converges later.

mistakes: Storing metadata and bytes in the same hash-partitioned system, then being unable to list by prefix.
Choosing erasure coding or replication without any durability or cost arithmetic.
Ignoring repair time, which dominates durability.
Making an object visible before its data is durable, or never cleaning up orphaned parts.

mid: Separated metadata (key → location) from the stored bytes
Used redundancy across racks or zones, not on one machine
Supported range reads and multipart upload for large files
Asked about object sizes and consistency needs first
senior: Computed raw capacity for replication versus erasure coding
Did a durability estimate with AFR and repair window, and got the order of magnitude right
Made the metadata commit the visibility point for strong read-after-write
Chose range partitioning for listing and handled hot ranges
Explained multipart complete as a metadata-only operation
staff: Showed that shrinking the repair window is the biggest durability lever (p³ scaling)
Addressed correlated failures: zones, racks, disk batches
Designed small-object packing and safe garbage collection
Stated CP for metadata and what fails during a partition
